items.excerpt: Synthtopia's take on I Am Choir: an AI vocal plug-in that generates ensemble choir performances from one recorded vocal, using voice models trained on consented, compensated session singers rather than scraped data.

Mastering The Mix launches MIXVAULT, an immersive EQ plug-in with a 3D room-style interface that analyses your audio and generates Smart Presets per source (mix, vocals, drums, bass), stepping through tonal directions from darker/fuller to brighter/more forward with level-matched monitoring.

MusicRadar's write-up of MIXVAULT frames it as a way to skip 'pesky hours of laborious EQing' — the plug-in's analysis engine proposes smart tonal starting points instead of manual band-by-band carving.

Empire Of The Sun's Luke Steele says 'of course' he uses AI, calling it 'like a really smart guitar pedal' and warning that artists who refuse it risk being swallowed by it — a working-artist framing of AI as just another studio effect in the chain.

Daft Punk's Thomas Bangalter says he's 'not really interested in the creative usage of AI', arguing the most interesting part of the creative process doesn't happen on an intellectual level at all — a direct counterpoint to the pro-AI producer camp.

A songwriter describes using Suno — with ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok to refine prompts — to finally hear lyrics he'd been writing for three decades, which led to real collaborations and close to 200,000 streams. A concrete look at prompt-driven songwriting as a working method.

The 'Human-First' badge spreading among independent artists has no verification behind it. The piece argues distributors should require granular AI-use disclosure at upload — which stems, which vocals, which tools — the way open source licences are defined and policed.

MIDiA's Tatiana Cirisano asks why, despite AI tracks flooding streaming uploads, none has produced an actual hit — and what that says about taste, fandom and the parts of music-making generative models still can't touch.
